name: Luxembourgish
family: Indo-European, Germanic, West Germanic, Central Franconian (Moselle Franconian)
variety: Central Luxembourgish (the Alzette valley and the city of Luxembourg), the emerging standard described by Gilles and Trouvain (2013)
sources: Gilles, Peter and Trouvain, Jürgen (2013). Luxembourgish. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 43(1), 67-74.
Gilles, Peter (1999). Dialektausgleich im Lëtzebuergeschen: Zur phonetisch-phonologischen Fokussierung einer Nationalsprache. Tübingen: Niemeyer.
Newton, Gerald (ed.) (1996). Luxembourg and Lëtzebuergesch: Language and Communication at the Crossroads of Europe. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
Grabe, Esther and Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the Rhythm Class Hypothesis. In Gussenhoven and Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
contrasts: short versus long vowels, mostly with a difference of quality as well: /ɑ/ versus /aː/ (Kapp, Kap), /i/ versus /iː/, /o/ versus /oː/, /u/ versus /uː/
three short front vowels /i e æ/ (midd, Méck, Bett)
pairs of closing diphthongs with a short and a long first element: /ɑɪ/ versus /æːɪ/ (Leit, Zäit) and /ɑʊ/ versus /æːʊ/ (Auto, Raum)
centring diphthongs /iə uə/ (hien, Buedem) and mid-centralised closing diphthongs /əɪ əʊ/ (schéin, Schoul)
fortis versus lenis obstruents, neutralised at the end of a word
alveolo-palatal [ɕ ʑ] versus postalveolar /ʃ ʒ/, a contrast that younger speakers are merging
lexical stress, mainly in loans from French
allophony: /χ ʁ/ are uvular or velar after back vowels and alveolo-palatal [ɕ ʑ] after front vowels and consonants (Buch [bux] or [buχ], Bicher [ˈbiɕɐ], Dag [daːχ], Deeg [deːɕ], Ligen [ˈliːʑən])
short /e/ is [e] before velar consonants (Méck, drécken) and a rounded, schwa-like [ə] elsewhere (written ë: Dëppen); this schwa-like vowel can be stressed

/ʀ/ is a uvular trill or fricative in onsets, is devoiced towards [χ] next to voiceless consonants, and is vocalised to [ɐ] in the coda, which gives the centring diphthongs of Dier, Joer, Stär; unstressed -er is [ɐ] (Kanner [ˈkɑnɐ])
/p t k/ are aspirated except after /s ʃ/; /b d ɡ/ are lenis and mostly voiceless
final fortition: obstruents are voiceless at the end of a word before a pause or a consonant
a word-final obstruent is voiced before a vowel-initial word in the same phrase, with resyllabification (sech eens [zəʑ ˈeːns])
written g between vowels and at the end of a word is a fricative: [ʑ] or [ʁ] between vowels, [ɕ] or [χ] finally (Vugel [ˈfuːʁəl], Bierg [biɐɕ])
final n is dropped before most consonants (the n-rule or Eifel rule) and kept before a vowel, a pause and n, d, t, z, h; the spelling shows it (den Dag but de Mann)
[w] occurs after consonants in the same onset (zwee [tsweː], schwaarz, Quell)
/eː oː/ are close, and /aː/ is a front or central vowel while short /ɑ/ is back
the nasal vowels and the front rounded vowels occur in loans from French and German (Restaurant, Chamber, Süden, blöd)
phonotactics: onset clusters as in German, with /ʃ/ before p, t, m, n, l, r, w (Stad, Sprooch, schwaarz) and initial /ts/
word-final obstruents are voiceless unless a vowel-initial word follows
final n is subject to the n-rule
short stressed vowels are followed by a consonant; after short vowels the spelling doubles the consonant but the consonant is not long
unstressed syllables of native words have [ə] or [ɐ]

stress.type: lexical, mostly initial in native words
stress.rule: Native words stress the first syllable of the stem, the prefixes ge-, be-, ver-, er-, ent-, zer- are unstressed, compounds stress their first member, and French loans are stressed on the last full syllable or, when integrated, on the first.
stress.cues: pitch movement, duration and intensity; unstressed native syllables have reduced vowels

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed native syllables have [ə] or [ɐ]; loans keep full vowels
rhythm.notes: Word stress and reduction are of the Germanic type, but Grabe and Low (2002), from one speaker, found a low vocalic nPVI together with a consonantal variability like that of German, and left the language unclassified.

length.notes: Vowel length is contrastive; long vowels are clearly longer than short ones, but I know of no published ratio. Consonants are not long; double consonant letters mark a short vowel.

intonation.declarative: accents with a peak on the stressed syllable and a final fall to low
intonation.wh_question: accent on the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise or high level at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: peak on the accented syllable followed by a fall
intonation.notes: Low confidence: I know of no detailed published account of Luxembourgish intonation that I can cite with certainty; the statements give the general West Germanic pattern.

tone.notes: The standard has no tone accents. The neighbouring Central Franconian dialects of Germany have two tone accents; Luxembourgish has no such contrast.

phonation: no contrastive phonation; vowel-initial words may begin with a glottal stop, but final consonants are usually linked to a following vowel instead

problems: there are no translator settings for lb, so stress follows the default penultimate rule, and neither lb_rules nor the 35,000 entries of lb_list mark stress: Lëtzebuerg and Lëtzebuerger are stressed on the second syllable, Gemeng on the prefix, Universitéit on the penultimate
unstressed -er and vocalised r are written with the consonant phoneme rR, a uvular fricative [ʁ], not with the vowel [ɐ]: Kanner is [kɑnʁ], Bäcker [bækʁ], Dier [diːʁ]
/æ/ (phoneme E) uses the same formant data as /e/ and /eː/ (vowel/e), so Bett and hell sound like [e]; every short and long pair shares one formant file and differs only in duration
the front rounded vowels y, y: and œː are built from diphthong data (vdiph2/uu@, vdiph2/o@) and /ɛː/ from vdiph/ae_2, so they glide instead of holding one quality

final devoicing is written into single rules only (d after a consonant, g, and entries of the list): a final b, v or z in a word outside the list stays voiced, and final obstruents are not voiced before a vowel-initial word
/s/ is declared voiced and built on the formants of [z] (FMT(voc/z)); the consonants have no formant transitions (Vowelin, Vowelout) and no length modifiers
the IPA names of two phonemes are wrong: the velar nasal is labelled retroflex [ɳ] and /χ/ is labelled with a capital X
function words carry stress in running text (den Hond ass do comes out with four stressed words), although the list marks a few of them as unstressed
questions are given the same tune whether they are yes-no or wh-questions
good: the diphthong inventory of the standard is complete, including the pairs with short and long first elements
alveolo-palatal [ɕ ʑ] and uvular or velar fricatives are distributed by the preceding vowel (Bicher, Buch, Ligen, Vugel)
a large pronunciation list covers the common vocabulary, including French loans with nasal vowels
initial st, sp have [ʃ]; z is [ts]

notes: In the consonant list [ɕ ʑ] are positional variants of /χ ʁ/ for speakers who keep them apart from /ʃ ʒ/, and [w] is the post-consonantal form of /v/. In the vowel list /y yː øː œː/ and the nasal vowels belong to loans, and [ɐ] is the vocalised form of /ʀ/ and of unstressed -er. The diphthongs iːɐ, uːɐ, ɛːɐ, oːɐ come from a long vowel plus vocalised r. No formant or voice onset time values are given because I cannot quote published figures with confidence.
